Let me carefully grade this write-up.

The problem is IMO 2026 Problem 1. The write-up needs to be graded on four mechanisms:
1. "answer" = explicit value of M: v_p(M) = gcd of valuations for every prime p, i.e., M = prod p^{gcd_i v_p(a_i)}. The write-up explicitly states this in Part (b): "M = prod_p p^{g_p}, g_p = gcd(v_p(a_1), ..., v_p(a_N))". That's explicit and correct. So answer = 2.

2. "reduction" = (E): elementary move description: for every prime p, valuations (x, y) → (min(x,y), |x-y|), and a move never outputs two 1s (at least one output > 1). The write-up has Lemma 1 with the valuations formula: v_p(g) = min(α,β), v_p(ℓ) = |α - β|. And it addresses the "never outputs two 1s": "Since m,n>1 we also have lcm(m,n)>1, whence at least one of g,ℓ is greater than 1." Actually more precisely: g·ℓ = lcm(m,n) > 1. Yes that's stated. So reduction = 2.

Wait, the (E) mechanism also requires the fact that the second output is mn/gcd > 1 when gcd = 1... The description in the grading key says: "a move never outputs two 1s (if gcd(m,n) = 1 the second output is mn > 1, otherwise the first output is gcd > 1)". The write-up says g·ℓ = lcm(m,n) ≥ max(m,n) > 1, so at least one of g, ℓ is > 1. That's a correct argument. So (E) is fully present. reduction = 2.

3. "lower_bound" = (T): termination and exactly one survivor for every play. The write-up uses the lexicographic potential (k, P) where k = number of entries > 1, P = product of all entries. Let me check the argument carefully.

The claim: every legal move strictly decreases (k, P) lexicographically. Hmm, is that actually true? Let's check.

Case 1: both g > 1 and ℓ > 1. Then k unchanged. New product = old product / g. For lexicographic decrease we need P to strictly decrease, i.e., g > 1. In this sub-case, if both g > 1 and ℓ > 1, then g ≥ 2, so new product = P/g ≤ P/2 < P. That's fine. Wait, but actually in this sub-case, is the new product P/g? Let's verify: the two entries m, n are replaced by g and ℓ. The product of new pair is g·ℓ = lcm(m,n) = mn/g. So the new total product P' = P · (gℓ)/(mn) = P · (mn/g)/(mn) = P/g. Yes. So in case 1, P' = P/g < P since g ≥ 2. Good.

Hmm, wait, but there's a subtle issue: the write-up's case 1 argument is confusing. It says "we cannot have g=1 (if g=1 then ℓ=lcm(m,n)=mn>1, but then...)" — there's a garbled passage: "but then the product of the new numbers would be ℓ=mn while the formula gℓ=mn/g forces g=1 and the product is unchanged — wait: if g=1 then exactly one of g,ℓ exceeds 1, namely ℓ)". This is a weird self-correcting passage, but the conclusion is right: in the sub-case where both g > 1 and ℓ > 1, we have g ≥ 2, so P' = P/g < P. The "wait" is a bit odd stylistically but the logic stands: in sub-case "both > 1", g > 1 by assumption, hence g ≥ 2, hence P' = P/g ≤ P/2 < P.

Actually hold on. Let me re-read: "Since g=gcd(m,n)≥1 and both replacement numbers exceed 1, we cannot have g=1 (if g=1 then ℓ=lcm(m,n)=mn>1, but then the product of the new numbers would be ℓ=mn while the formula gℓ=mn/g forces g=1 and the product is unchanged — wait: if g=1 then exactly one of g,ℓ exceeds 1, namely ℓ)."

So the argument: in this sub-case both g and ℓ exceed 1, so g ≠ 1 (since g exceeds 1), hence g ≥ 2, hence P' = P/g ≤ P/2 < P. The parenthetical is confusing but the final conclusion "Thus in the present sub-case we necessarily have g≥2, so the new product P′ satisfies P′=P/g≤P/2<P" is correct.

Case 2: exactly one of g, ℓ exceeds 1. Then k drops by 1. Fine for lexicographic decrease (first component drops).

Case 3: neither exceeds 1: impossible since gℓ = lcm ≥ max(m,n) > 1.

So every move strictly decreases (k, P) in lexicographic order on N × N_{>0}. Wait, is lexicographic order on N × N_{>0} well-founded? Yes: there's no infinite strictly decreasing sequence in lexicographic order on N × N (with first component from N = non-negative integers). Actually, hmm: lexicographic order on N × N is well-founded? Yes. A strictly decreasing sequence (k_1, P_1) > (k_2, P_2) > ... : the first components form a non-increasing sequence of naturals, so eventually constant; then the second components form a strictly decreasing sequence of naturals, which must be finite. So yes, termination holds. The write-up says "Since k is a non-negative integer and P is a positive integer, there can be only finitely many successive decreases." That's a valid (if terse) well-foundedness argument. Fine.

Hmm, but wait: there's a subtlety. Is it true that every move decreases (k,P) lexicographically? Consider case 1: both outputs > 1. Then k stays the same, and P decreases. Case 2: exactly one output > 1: k decreases by 1. Lexicographic: (k-1, P') < (k, P) regardless of P'. Yes. So the monovariant works.

Actually wait, is there an issue: in case 2, could P' be... doesn't matter. Lexicographic.

But hold on: is there a possible issue with case 1 when g=1? If g = 1, then ℓ = lcm(m,n) = mn > 1 (since m, n > 1, coprime). So exactly one of g, ℓ exceeds 1 — that's case 2, not case 1. So case 1 indeed has g ≥ 2. Correct.

Then, at termination, k ≤ 1 (at most one entry > 1, else a move is possible). Need k ≥ 1: the write-up argues that a move never decreases k below 1: "the only way k can drop is the second sub-case above, in which exactly one of the two replacement numbers exceeds 1; thus after that move we still have k_new = k_old - 1 ≥ 1 whenever k_old ≥ 2."

Hmm, wait. Is that argument complete? In sub-case 2, k decreases by exactly 1. In sub-case 1, k is unchanged. So if k_old ≥ 2, k_new ≥ k_old - 1 ≥ 1. And if k_old = 1... can a move even be made when k_old = 1? A move requires two entries > 1, so k_old ≥ 2 for a legal move. So k never drops below 1: k_new = k_old - 1 ≥ 1 when a move occurs (since k_old ≥ 2). Correct. Also, at termination k ≤ 1 and k ≥ 1, so k = 1. 

Also, alternatively the "at least one output > 1" fact: from g·ℓ = lcm(m,n) > 1. Yes.

So (T) seems complete: termination via lexicographic monovariant, and exactly one survivor. The grading rubric says: "termination proved but the 'at least one number stays > 1' step missing or circular" would score 1. Here the step is present. The parenthetical alternative argument in the write-up is convoluted, but the main argument ("from g·ℓ=lcm(m,n)>1 a move always leaves at least one entry >1 among the two it writes, so when two entries >1 are replaced the number of entries >1 drops by at most 1 and cannot jump from 2 directly to 0") is present and correct. Actually, hmm, let me double check: k_new = k_old - 1 in sub-case 2 — this counts: two entries > 1 removed, one entry > 1 inserted, so net -1. Since a move requires k_old ≥ 2, k_new ≥ 1. Yes.

But wait — one more check on the termination argument. Is the claim "every legal move strictly decreases (k, P) lexicographically" fully proven? Case 1: P' = P/g < P. Case 2: k decreases. Yes, that's all cases (case 3 impossible). Good.

Actually, hold on, one more subtlety about case 1: "From (eq:prod) the new product equals the old product divided by g." Check: new product = P - mn + gℓ... i.e., P' = P · gℓ/(mn) = P/(g) since gℓ = mn/g. Yes. And g ≥ 2 gives P' ≤ P/2 < P. Good.

So lower_bound = 2.

Hmm, but wait: the rubric mentions as an example of a false lemma: "relying on a false lemma such as 'the product of the board strictly decreases at every move'". The write-up does NOT rely on that; it correctly uses the lexicographic pair because P can increase when g = 1 (P' = P in that case... wait, if g = 1, P' = P/1 = P, so P unchanged, not increased). Actually P never increases: P' = P/g ≤ P. When g = 1, P' = P. Hmm, so actually the product never increases, and it strictly decreases when g > 1; when g = 1, k decreases by 1. That's exactly the rubric's suggested monovariant. The write-up uses the lexicographic pair, which is equivalent and correct.

4. "upper_bound" = (I): invariance of valuation gcds for every move and every prime p, handling equal valuations and zero valuations. Lemma 2: multiset S, replace α, β by min(α,β) and |α-β|; gcd unchanged. Proof: d = gcd(S) divides α, β, hence divides min(α,β) and |α-β| (since d | α and d | β implies d | min and d | difference — careful: min(α,β) is either α or β, so yes). Conversely, any common divisor d' of the new multiset divides the two new numbers min and |α-β|, hence their sum = max(α,β) and... hmm, "their difference (which equals |α-β|)". Wait: sum of min(α,β) and |α-β| = max(α,β). Difference = |α - β|... hmm, the difference of min and |α-β| is... |min(α,β) - |α-β||. If α ≤ β: min = α, |α-β| = β-α; difference = |α - (β-α)| = |2α - β|. Hmm, that's not |α-β|. But actually we don't need the difference: from d' | α (min) and d' | (β - α) (difference of original), we get d' | β = α + (β-α). The write-up says: "any common divisor of the new multiset divides both new numbers and therefore divides their sum (which equals max(α,β)) and their difference (which equals |α-β|), hence divides both α and β."

Hmm, "their difference (which equals |α-β|)" — the difference of the two new numbers min and |α-β| equals |α-β| only if min(α,β) ≤ |α-β|... Actually |min - |α-β||. If α ≤ β: min = α, |α-β| = β-α. If β-α ≥ α, difference = β-2α; not β-α in general. So the parenthetical claim about "their difference" is wrong-ish. But it doesn't matter: we only need the sum: min + |α-β| = max(α,β). Then α = min, β = max, and both are recoverable from the two new numbers: the new numbers are min and |α-β|; the common divisor d' divides min (= one of α, β) and divides min + |α-β| = max, hence divides both α and β. So the argument works via sum alone. The "difference" statement is redundant and slightly incorrect as stated, but the essential step (divides sum = max, and one of the new numbers is min = the smaller of α, β... wait, is min(α,β) necessarily equal to α or β? Yes, by definition min(α,β) ∈ {α, β}.) Hmm, but for the proof: d' divides min and |α-β|; hence d' divides min + |α-β| = max(α,β); and min(α,β), max(α,β) are α, β in some order. So d' divides α and β. Correct. The extra mention of "their difference" is harmless (it's actually also true that d' divides |α-β| trivially since that IS one of the new numbers — I think the write-up meant that d' divides the difference of the original pair, i.e., |α-β|, which is one of the new numbers). So the proof is fine.

Zero valuations: gcd conventions stated in Corollary 3: "gcd of an empty set is 0 and gcd(0,a) = a". Also gcd(0,0) = 0 by convention presumably. Lemma 2's proof handles α or β = 0 fine (divisibility arguments work). Equal valuations: α = β gives new pair (α, 0); gcd(α, 0) = α = gcd(α, β). The proof: d' divides min = α and |α-β| = 0; sum = α = max; so d' divides α = β. Fine. So Lemma 2 covers all cases.

Then Corollary 3: for every prime p, g_p = gcd of valuations on board is invariant. Then part (b): terminal board has one M > 1 and rest 1s, so g_p = v_p(M), hence v_p(M) = initial g_p, determined by initial board. Explicit formula given: M = prod p^{gcd(v_p(a_1),...,v_p(a_N))}. So upper_bound = 2.

Now, is there any flaw? Let me double-check Lemma 1: v_p(ℓ) = max - min = |α - β|. Correct: lcm/gcd, valuations subtract. And gcd(min(α,β), |α-β|) = gcd(α,β): proof by assuming α ≤ β, new pair (α, β - α), gcd(α, β-α) = gcd(α, β). Correct.

Lemma 2 combined with Lemma 1 gives invariance of g_p. Good.

One more check: in part (b), they use "gcd(v_p(M), 0, ..., 0) = v_p(M)". Fine.

The "answer": explicit M = ∏_p p^{g_p}, g_p = gcd(v_p(a_1),...,v_p(a_N)). Explicit and correct. answer = 2.
